chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: White patronage of Harlem, after-hours joints and copied riffs
summary: In the early thirties whites flocked safely to Harlem clubs and after-hours spots, and downtown musicians wrote down riffs on their cuffs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Oh, definitely. And, you know, a lot of them used to come up to Harlem back in the early thirties, you know, when a lot of white musicians and white people used to come up to Harlem to hang out. There was no muggings. Nobody bothered anybody in those days. And Harlem was a beautiful place. A lot of night clubs there and it was patronized mostly by whites. The Cotton Club. Connie's Inn. Small's Paradise, some colored used to go there. And the Saratoga Club, you see. But mostly the patronage was white.
Yeah, the clientele that had the money to spend.

And there used to be a lot of after-hour joints, you know, up there from 133rd Street on up to 140th Street. Between Seventh and Lenox there was a lot of afterhour joints up there that had piano players. Guys used to go in and jam. There was a 101 Club there near Lenox Avenue, I think at 141st Street, that white musicians used to come up and jam and, you know, that way and play.

Then, you see, Milt, I can tell you something else, too. I remember being with Don Redmon's band when musicians used to sit, they'd come uptown and they'd have their tuxedo on with a stiff collar and cuffs and they would make a staff on their cuff and you'd play a riff and they'd write that down, you see.
A lot of things went downtown that way, too.
: They would copy the creativity -- notate, rather, --
: -- the creativity of jazz musicians, black jazz musicians.
Uh-huh, but the records helped a lot, too.
